pecheur_simple.intro: Joins two cords or two lines of the same thickness, simply and securely.
etapes: Lay the two ends side by side, pointing in opposite directions.
With the first end, tie an overhand knot around the other cord.
With the second end, tie an overhand knot around the first cord.
Pull both cords: the two knots slide towards each other and lock.
attention: To bear a person's weight, prefer the double fisherman's knot.
pecheur_simple.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

sang.intro: The fishing knot for joining two fine nylon lines without slipping.
etapes: Cross the two lines over about ten centimetres.
Wrap the first end 5 times around the other line, then bring it back between the two lines, at the crossing point.
Wrap the second end 5 times around the first line, in the other direction.
Pass this second end through the same central gap, but in the opposite direction to the first.
Wet it, pull the two lines slowly, then trim the ends.
sang.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

roulant.intro: It grips a pole or another rope and doesn't slip when pulled lengthwise. For pulling a log, taking the strain off a loaded rope or tensioning a tarp.
etapes: Pass the end around the pole, crossing the standing part, on the side you'll pull towards.
Make a second turn next to the first, crossing the standing part again, still on the pulling side.
Pass the end around the pole on the other side of the standing part and tuck it under itself.
Tighten, then pull lengthwise, on the side of the two turns.
roulant.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

hune.intro: Fixes a rope to an eyelet or ring that keeps moving, like a tarp flapping in the wind: it tightens instead of loosening.
etapes: Pass the end through the eyelet or ring.
With the end, make a turn around the standing part.
Make a second turn around the standing part, between the first turn and the ring.
Tuck the end under this second turn: it's a clove hitch tied around the standing part.
Tighten by pulling the standing part.
attention: Very hard to untie after a heavy load.
hune.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

levier.intro: Slip a stick into a rope to make a handle: for pulling hard, tightening a lashing or making the rungs of a rope ladder.
etapes: Make a loop in the rope.
Fold it back over the standing part.
Slide the stick over the sides of the loop and under the standing part.
Pull: the rope locks on the stick. To release, remove the stick.
levier.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

bachmann.intro: A friction hitch with a carabiner: the carabiner acts as a handle to slide it. Practical with gloves or cold hands.
etapes: Clip a loop of cord into a carabiner.
Hold the carabiner flat against the main rope, gate facing out.
Wrap the cord 3 or 4 times around the rope and the back of the carabiner, working upwards, passing through the carabiner each time.
Load the cord loop downwards: the knot locks. Push the carabiner to move it.
attention: It only locks when pulled downwards. Never grab the turns during a fall: the knot would no longer lock.
bachmann.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

chaise_tours.intro: A safer bowline: the doubled central loop grips the rope better, especially if it's slippery or stiff.
etapes: Make two small loops on top of each other instead of one, the working end passing over the top.
Pass the working end up through both loops from underneath.
Take it behind the standing part.
Bring it back down through both loops.
Tighten and leave a tail of at least 10 cm.
chaise_tours.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

boucle_simple.intro: The quickest loop to tie, for a light load: hanging a bag, a bottle or a drying line.
etapes: Fold the end of the rope into a bight.
Tie an overhand knot with this doubled section.
Tighten by pulling the loop and both strands.
attention: It jams and weakens the rope: for a real load, prefer the figure-eight loop.
boucle_simple.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

chainette.intro: Shortens and stores a long rope without tangles, and unravels it in one go.
etapes: Make a loop near the end of the rope.
Pull a bight of the standing part through this loop.
Pull a new bight through the previous one, and carry on like this along the whole length.
To lock it, pass the end through the last bight. To undo it, pull the end out and pull: everything unravels.
chainette.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

tresse.intro: Makes a stronger cord from thin strands: nettle fibres, lime bark, grasses, string.
etapes: Tie the three strands together at one end, or wedge them under a stone.
Pass the right strand over the middle one: it becomes the middle strand.
Pass the left strand over the new middle strand.
Repeat, alternating right and left, tightening evenly.
Add a new strand by overlapping it for a few centimetres when one gets short. Finish with an overhand knot.
tresse.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

filet.intro: With cord, a net can serve as a hammock, a carrying bag or a drying rack.
etapes: Stretch a head rope between two trees.
Attach equal lengths of cord to it at regular intervals, with lark's heads.
Tie each strand to its neighbour with an overhand knot, all at the same height: that's the first row of meshes.
Next row: shift by half a mesh and tie each strand to its other neighbour.
Carry on row after row, keeping the meshes the same size, then tie the bottom onto a second rope.
attention: Fishing or hunting with a net is forbidden in most European countries.
filet.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

epissure_oeil.intro: A permanent loop at the end of a three-strand rope, stronger than any knot.
etapes: Unlay the three strands for about 15 cm and whip the end of each one.
Fold the rope to form the eye of the size you want.
Tuck the middle strand under one strand of the standing part, against the lay.
Tuck the left strand under the next strand of the standing part, to the left of the first.
Turn the splice over and tuck the last strand under the remaining free strand of the standing part.
Carry on: each strand goes over one strand and under the next. Make at least 5 tucks, then trim the ends.
attention: Only for laid rope (visible strands), not for braided climbing rope.
epissure_oeil.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

epissure_arriere.intro: Finishes the end of a three-strand rope neatly so it never frays.
etapes: Unlay the strands for about ten centimetres.
Make a crown: fold each strand over its neighbour, in the same direction, and pass the last one through the loop of the first. Tighten.
Tuck each strand back towards the rope, over one strand and under the next, against the lay.
Make 3 tucks with each strand.
Roll the splice under your foot to settle it, then trim the ends.
epissure_arriere.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

epissure_courte.intro: Repairs a cut three-strand rope, or joins two, without a knot: the join stays strong.
etapes: Unlay the strands of both ends for about 15 cm and whip the end of each strand.
Interlock the two ends: each strand of one rope sits between two strands of the other.
Temporarily tie the centre with string so it holds.
On one side, tuck each strand over one strand and under the next, against the lay. Make 3 tucks.
Remove the temporary tie and do the same on the other side.
Roll the splice under your foot to settle it, then trim the ends.
attention: The splice thickens the rope: it will no longer run through a small pulley.
epissure_courte.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

surliure_francaise.intro: Another way of finishing the end of a rope, or making a non-slip grip on a handle, with a series of half hitches.
etapes: Tie the thin thread onto the rope with an overhand knot.
Make a half hitch around the rope and pull it tight against the knot.
Make the next one right beside it, always in the same direction: the knots form a small spiral ridge.
Carry on for a length equal to 1.5 times the diameter, or along the whole handle.
Finish with two tight half hitches and cut the thread.
surliure_francaise.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

noeuds_eviter.intro: The reef knot has two false twins that fail under load: the granny knot and the thief knot. Knowing how to recognise them avoids a nasty surprise.
etapes: Correct reef knot: left over right, then right over left. Both ends come out on the same side and the knot is nicely symmetrical.
Granny knot: left over right twice. The ends come out at an angle, the knot is twisted and it slips.
Thief knot: it looks like the reef knot, but the two ends come out diagonally, on opposite sides. It fails very easily.
If in doubt, untie it and tie it again saying out loud: “left over right, right over left”.
noeuds_eviter.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska

partir_leger.intro: The old principle of the backwoodsmen: every item must earn its weight. A light pack tires you less, and you stay sharper.
etapes: Spread all your gear on the floor before leaving and weigh the pack.
For each item, ask yourself: “Did I use it last time? Does another item already do the same job?”
Keep first what's hard to make outdoors: a cutting tool, shelter, a way to make fire, a water container, cord.
Choose items that do several jobs (the pot is also a bowl, the tarp is also a rain collector).
Share the group gear among the members, so nobody carries everything.
Weigh the pack when you get back and note what wasn't used: that's the list of what you'll leave behind next time.
attention: Light, but never without the safety minimum: something to warm you, signal and treat yourself.
partir_leger.source: Inspired by Nessmuk (1884), Kephart (1906) and Beard (1920), public-domain works, rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

habits_couches.intro: Two thin garments keep warmth better than one thick one: the air trapped between them insulates.
etapes: Next to the skin: wool or synthetic. Never cotton, which stays wet and cold when you sweat.
On top: one or two thin warm layers (fleece, wool), easy to take off.
Outside: a wind and rain jacket, loose enough to go over everything else.
A collar that turns up, a hat and gloves: you lose a lot of comfort through the neck and extremities.
Keep a dry outfit just for the night, packed in a waterproof bag.
Take off a layer before you sweat, going uphill, and put it back on as soon as you stop.
habits_couches.source: Inspired by Nessmuk (1884), Kephart (1906) and Beard (1920), public-domain works, rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

secher.intro: Damp things mean a cold night and blisters the next day. But too close to the fire, leather cracks and synthetics melt.
etapes: Stuff wet shoes with dry grass, leaves or paper, and change it every hour: it soaks up the water from the inside.
Dry things in moving air, on a branch at a safe distance from the fire: you should be able to hold your hand in the same spot comfortably.
Never put shoes or synthetic clothing against hot stones or above the flames.
Damp socks and gloves: slip them under your jacket or into the sleeping bag, against you. Your warmth dries them overnight.
In the morning, shake the sleeping bag and air it: it holds your body's moisture.
secher.source: Inspired by Nessmuk (1884), Kephart (1906) and Beard (1920), public-domain works, rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

affuter.intro: A tool that cuts well is a safer tool: it slips less and needs less force.
etapes: Bring a small sharpening stone or plate, one coarse side and one fine side.
Wet the stone, lay the blade flat then raise the spine about 20° (the thickness of two coins under the spine).
Slide the blade as if cutting a thin slice off the stone, from heel to tip, the same number of times on each side.
Finish on the fine side, then on a leather belt or your trousers, spine of the blade first.
Wrap a little waxed string or tape around the hatchet's handle: the grip stays secure with wet hands.
Wipe and dry the blade every evening; a drop of cooking oil is enough against rust.
attention: Always cut outwards, never towards your leg or hand. Kneel for the hatchet: if it bounces, it hits the ground and not your shin.
affuter.source: Inspired by Nessmuk (1884), Kephart (1906) and Beard (1920), public-domain works, rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

ustensiles.intro: With a knife and dead wood, you can make in minutes whatever is missing around the fire.
etapes: Poker: a dry stick about 1 m long, as thick as two fingers, flattened at the end, with a notch for lifting a pot's handle.
Ember tongs: a flexible stick a finger thick, thinned in the middle, warmed gently near the embers then bent in two. Trim both ends so they meet.
Fork: a small forked branch, peeled and sharpened.
Spatula and spoon: a board split from sound dead wood, hollowed out with the tip of the knife.
Camp broom: fallen twigs tied around a stick, for sweeping the fire area and the shelter floor.
ustensiles.source: Inspired by Nessmuk (1884), Kephart (1906) and Beard (1920), public-domain works, rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

silex.intro: The old-timers' method: a hard stone and a piece of steel throw sparks that catch on prepared tinder.
etapes: Find a hard stone with a sharp edge: flint, quartz, chert. Soft stones (limestone, slate) don't work.
Take a piece of carbon steel: a fire striker, an old file, or the spine of a non-stainless steel knife.
Lay a piece of char cloth or tinder fungus on the stone, held with your thumb, 1 mm below the edge.
Strike the edge of the stone with the steel, a sharp scraping blow downwards, at about 45°.
When a spark catches on the tinder (a small red dot), blow on it gently.
Slip it into a nest of dry fibres and blow until it flames.
attention: Steel sparks are cool: they only catch on very dry, charred tinder (Char cloth sheet).
silex.source: Inspired by Nessmuk (1884), Kephart (1906) and Beard (1920), public-domain works, rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

amadou_naturel.intro: Tinder is what turns a spark into a flame. The forest offers it everywhere, as long as you keep it dry.
etapes: Birch bark: the thin white outer layers burn even when damp thanks to their oil. Take them from a dead tree or the ground.
Dry grass and fibres: dead grass, old man's beard (clematis), bulrush down, fibres of the inner bark of dead wood, rubbed between your hands.
Dry puffball: the brown powder of an old, dry puffball takes sparks.
Resinous wood shavings: scrape the inside of a dead pine stump with your knife, very rich in resin.
Keep everything in a waterproof box or bag, and gather tinder as you walk whenever you come across some.
attention: Don't take bark from a living tree: you injure it. And don't take bird or rodent nests.
amadou_naturel.source: Inspired by Nessmuk (1884), Kephart (1906) and Beard (1920), public-domain works, rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

feu_neige.intro: A fire laid on snow sinks and goes out in its own water. It needs a floor.
etapes: Tread down the snow over a circle a metre across.
Lay a floor of dry dead wood: a layer of sticks packed side by side, then a second layer crosswise.
Build the fire on this floor, with plenty of kindling prepared in advance.
Shield it from the wind with a tarp, a rock or a row of logs.
Regularly add logs to the floor as it burns away.
attention: Never light a fire under a snow-laden tree: the heat brings it down in one block onto the fire.
feu_neige.source: Inspired by Nessmuk (1884), Kephart (1906) and Beard (1920), public-domain works, rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

feu_trois_buches.intro: An economical fire that lasts: three big logs meet in the centre, and you push them in as they burn.
etapes: Light a small, lively fire.
Arrange three logs of dead wood around it, like the spokes of a star, their ends in the embers.
For more heat, push the logs towards the centre. For less, pull them apart.
At night, push them together just before sleeping: the fire smoulders until morning.
feu_trois_buches.source: Inspired by Nessmuk (1884), Kephart (1906) and Beard (1920), public-domain works, rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

feu_pierre.titre: Fire on rock: beware of stones
feu_pierre.intro: A damp or porous stone can burst when it heats up and throw out fragments.
etapes: Avoid river pebbles and stones that have been soaking in water.
On a rock slab, first spread a layer of earth or sand a few centimetres thick.
For a stone ring, choose dry stones taken well away from water.
Don't sit with your back to a rock face heated by the fire.
feu_pierre.source: Inspired by Nessmuk (1884), Kephart (1906) and Beard (1920), public-domain works, rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

feu_cuisine.intro: You cook on embers, not flames: flames blacken pots, burn the outside and leave the inside raw.
etapes: Light your fire 30 to 45 minutes before cooking, with hardwood if possible (oak, beech, ash).
Lay two parallel logs, the width of your pot apart: they support it and keep the embers in the middle.
Let the wood turn into a bed of red embers.
Keep a small fire going alongside to produce new embers, and rake them under the pot with a stick.
For tea or coffee water, put the pot on the embers, not in the smoke: otherwise it will taste of smoke.
feu_cuisine.source: Inspired by Nessmuk (1884), Kephart (1906) and Beard (1920), public-domain works, rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

cremaillere.intro: For hanging a pot over the fire and adjusting the height, without putting anything in the embers.
etapes: Drive two forked sticks into the ground on either side of the fire, about 70 cm apart.
Lay a crossbar in the two forks, above the fire.
Simple hook: a small forked branch turned upside down, hung from the crossbar, with a notch at the bottom for the handle.
Adjustable hook: a stick with several notches cut at different heights. Change notch to raise or lower the pot.
One-stick version: push a long stick into the ground at an angle, its end above the fire, and wedge its base with a big stone.
attention: Use dead wood thick enough not to catch fire: check it regularly.
cremaillere.source: Inspired by Nessmuk (1884), Kephart (1906) and Beard (1920), public-domain works, rewritten and adapted for Bivaska
